text: This lesson assembles everything from Chapters 2 and 3 into one named architecture, a Variational Quantum Classifier. Every piece, encoding, ansatz, measurement, loss, optimizer, has already been introduced individually; here they combine into a complete, working pipeline.

A Variational Quantum Classifier has exactly four stages. Encode classical features into a quantum state using Lesson 10's angle or amplitude encoding. Apply the trainable ansatz from Lesson 6. Measure an observable, commonly Pauli-Z on one qubit, to get an expectation value between negative one and one. And convert that to a prediction, compute the loss, then use the parameter-shift rule and a classical optimizer to update the parameters.

Converting the expectation value to a prediction uses a simple rescale: p equals the expectation value plus one, divided by two. If a trained circuit outputs 0.6, p works out to 1.6 over 2, equal to 0.8 — predicted class 1 with 80 percent confidence. If it outputs negative 0.2, p is 0.8 over 2, equal to 0.4, below the 0.5 threshold, so predicted class 0.

Computing binary cross-entropy loss by hand: for a true label of 1 and a predicted probability of 0.8, the loss is negative log of 0.8, about 0.2231, a small, expected loss for a well-calibrated correct prediction. Compare that to the same true label with a confidently wrong-leaning prediction of 0.4: the loss jumps to negative log of 0.4, about 0.9163, more than four times larger, correctly penalizing the worse prediction much more heavily.

Next lesson covers a different QML approach entirely: quantum kernel methods, where the quantum computer's only job is computing a similarity measure between data points, handed off to a completely classical support vector machine.
